title: Keep the fraud-scoring client inside the vendor's session limit

blocks.text: The checkout scores every card payment with a fraud-scoring vendor. The contract allows this client a fixed number of calls in progress at once; when no session comes free within a short wait, the call is refused with `Busy` and checkout falls back to its offline rules.

The client has been in production for a month, and the incidents have gone both ways. After a morning of vendor errors, every checkout thread sat waiting for a session while the vendor saw no traffic at all. Two weeks later, during a busy evening when many calls were refused and many checkouts were abandoned while waiting, the vendor reported that the client had gone over its limit and throttled it.

Write `score(...)` in `src/main/java/practice/ScoringClient.java`. When you're done, the client never has more calls in progress than the contract allows and never fewer sessions than it is owed, whether a call is scored, fails at the vendor, is refused, or is cancelled while it waits. About six lines in total.
The tests run real threads against a vendor whose calls stay open until the test lets them finish. A cancelled checkout is cancelled through its `Future`, which interrupts the waiting thread.

cases.says: no more calls than the session limit reach the vendor at once, and calls beyond it wait and are all scored
a call that fails at the vendor gives its session back, so later calls still get one
a call refused because no session came free does not add a session
a call cancelled while it waits for a session neither takes nor adds a session

origin.section: A Semaphore Has No Owner and Trusts Every Release: Release Exactly What You Acquired

concepts: A permit is released in a finally, and only on the path where the acquire succeeded; a missed release shrinks the limit and a release without an acquire raises it.
